planting.note: Sow directly as early as soil can be worked, or start under cold frame protection for an even earlier crop, since it tolerates light frost well.

This German heirloom butterhead, also called Maikönig or May King, dates to before the 1880s and was bred to be the very first lettuce ready in spring, producing tender, rosy-blushed rosettes in under two months. Market gardeners historically relied on it to fill the earliest gap in the spring salad season.

planting.note: Sow in successive batches from spring through summer, since it holds its tender texture and mild flavor in warm weather far longer than typical soft-head lettuces.

directions: Sow in successive batches from spring through summer, since it holds its tender texture and mild flavor in warm weather far longer than typical soft-head lettuces. Developed near Kagran outside Vienna, this Austrian heirloom butterhead is prized for exceptional heat tolerance and slow bolting, unusual traits among classic butterheads. It remains a benchmark variety for gardeners needing a butterhead that survives real summer heat.

planting.note: Sow directly in early spring and again in late summer, since it resists bolting better than most soft-leaf lettuces.

directions: Sow directly in early spring and again in late summer, since it resists bolting better than most soft-leaf lettuces and holds quality through warm spells. A French Batavian heirloom dating to the 1880s, Trocadero forms loose, crunchy pale-green heads with a crisp, sweet, faintly nutty flavor reminiscent of iceberg but grown far more easily. It was long grown in French market gardens as a reliable source of crisp texture without the fuss of true crisphead types.

planting.note: Sow directly in the cool season; notably slow to bolt, suited to late-spring and early-summer sowings.

directions: Sow directly in the cool season; this heirloom Batavia lettuce from southern France, its name loosely translating to crunchy one of the Midi, produces elongated, savoyed, crisp heads bred to withstand the hot, dry summers of Provence. It is notably slow to bolt, making it well suited to late-spring and early-summer sowings when many other lettuces would turn bitter. Heirloom seed houses reintroduced it to American gardeners as a heat-season alternative to iceberg.

planting.note: Sow directly and thin to full spacing so heads can size up over a long, cool growing season.

directions: Sow directly and thin to full spacing so heads can size up over a long, cool growing season, since it matures more slowly than modern hybrid icebergs. Introduced by the Webbs seed company of Stourbridge, England, in the early twentieth century, this crisphead forms large, dense, frilly-edged pale green heads with a satisfying crunch and is long considered one of England's finest garden icebergs. It remains a staple of British allotments, valued for standing in the garden without premature bolting.
